title: Trump Says Pro-Israel Lobby's Power Is Fading — and Takes a Jab at Schumer
summary: In a pre-taped interview with the hyper-partisan show "America Speaks" on Real America's Voice, President Donald Trump made a striking claim: pro-Israel lobbying groups no longer hold the sway they once did in Washington. "If you go back 20, 25 years ago, they had the most powerful lobby in Washington," Trump said. "Now, everyone is... if you look at the House... you look at the Democrats in the House... it's pretty amazing actually." The comments come amid a broader shift in American politics. A recent AP-NORC survey found that support for Israel is eroding, especially among Democrats, with growing polarization even within the Republican base. Trump also took a swipe at Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, the highest-ranking Jewish official in U.S. history and a traditionally staunch supporter of Israel. "Look at Schumer. He's become virtually a Palestinian," Trump said. This isn't the first time he's used that phrase — he made similar remarks in 2025, both in the Oval Office and at the White House Correspondents' Dinner. The comments drew widespread condemnation from Jewish and Muslim groups, who saw them as a xenophobic slur, using "Palestinian" as a political insult. Schumer has recently been more critical of Israel, particularly its conduct in Gaza and the war with Iran. He called Netanyahu "too willing to tolerate the civilian toll in Gaza" and described the administration's approach to Iran as a "recipe for utter disaster." Trump's remarks highlight a real shift: the once-unshakeable pro-Israel consensus in Congress is showing cracks, and even the president acknowledges it.
why_it_matters: This story reveals how a long-standing bipartisan foreign policy consensus is breaking down, and how political leaders can turn identity labels into insults. For young people watching U.S. politics, it raises questions about how lawmakers balance foreign alliances, ethnic identity, and domestic polarization.

keywords.explanation: Hyper-partisan means strongly favoring one political party and framing information in a very one-sided way.
Eroding means gradually weakening or wearing away over time.
Polarization is the process by which two sides become sharply divided and less willing to compromise.
A xenophobic slur is an insult that attacks someone by treating a national or ethnic identity as a bad thing.
The Senate Minority Leader is the top senator in the party that does not control the Senate majority.
Consensus is a broad agreement shared by most people in a group.

background_read: President Donald Trump (who served as U.S. president from 2017 to 2021 and returned to office in 2025) made the remarks in a pre-taped interview on Real America's Voice, a conservative media outlet.
Chuck Schumer (a New York Democrat and the Senate Minority Leader) is the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in U.S. history and has represented New York in the Senate since 1999.
For decades, pro-Israel lobbying groups were considered among the most powerful forces in Washington, and their influence depended on strong bipartisan support in Congress.
That consensus has weakened as U.S. politics became more polarized over Middle East policy, especially during recent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran.
The AP-NORC survey cited in the article is conducted by the Associated Press and NORC at the University of Chicago, a nonpartisan research organization that measures public opinion.

perspectives.description: Some Trump allies and pro-Palestinian advocacy groups see the remark as an admission that pro-Israel lobbying is no longer immune to criticism. They believe this shift gives more space for open debate about U.S. policy toward Israel and Palestinians.

Jewish and Muslim organizations condemn the use of 'Palestinian' as an insult, arguing it treats an identity as a slur. Critics also say attacking Schumer's ethnic or religious identity distracts from actual policy disagreements about Gaza and Iran.

Polling analysts see Trump's comment as part of a measurable shift: AP-NORC data shows support for Israel eroding among Democrats while Republicans polarize. The Senate itself reflects an older bipartisan consensus cracking along generational and ideological lines.

The question ahead is whether this breakdown will reshape U.S. foreign policy toward Israel, Palestine, and Iran. Schumer's position may be an early indicator of how Democratic leaders balance long-standing alliances with growing progressive pressure.
